title: eLocust3m and AI data cleaning feed FAO's East Africa locust control, which may have averted USD 1.56 billion in losses
summary: PlantVillage's app, built with FAO in under a month in 2020, gathered 240,000+ records; AI removed unusable data; FAO credits the tech-enabled operation with averting USD 1.56 billion in losses.
account: In early 2020 desert locust swarms swept the Horn of Africa. FAO's senior locust forecaster Keith Cressman asked Penn State's PlantVillage to adapt its app. PlantVillage had built FAO's fall armyworm app. eLocust3M was released on Google Play on 20 February 2020. Anyone with a smartphone could record georeferenced locust sightings; algorithms checked photos. Penn State also extended a deep-learning soil-moisture model to the affected region. FAO reported receiving up to 2,500 records a day, nearly 25 percent unusable or incorrect. It asked PlantVillage to use artificial intelligence to identify and remove the unwanted data before sharing locations with ground and air control teams. The New York Times reported over 240,000 records collected in a year by PlantVillage scouts, government personnel and citizens. The wider operation also used Garmin satellite devices, EarthRanger (Vulcan) and 28 aircraft coordinated with 51 Degrees. FAO's 6 May 2021 feature says East African control operations prevented the loss of 4 million tonnes of cereal and 800 million liters of milk. They protected 36.6 million people's food security and avoided USD 1.56 billion in losses, it says. The Times quoted FAO's estimate of USD 1.5 billion averted since February 2020. It quoted FAO's Cyril Ferrand saying swarms were prevented from spilling into the Sahel.
purpose: Collect georeferenced locust sightings from anyone with a smartphone. Automatically check photos and remove unusable records so that FAO can direct survey and control teams.
system: eLocust3m (PlantVillage) with AI data validation feeding FAO's Desert Locust Information Service
developer: PlantVillage, Pennsylvania State University, with FAO
deployer: FAO Desert Locust Information Service and national locust control operations in Kenya, Ethiopia and Somalia
taxonomy_note: The AI cleaned one data stream in a wider operation, and the averted-loss figure is FAO's estimate for the whole effort.

ratings.reason: FAO states that East African control operations prevented the loss of 4 million tonnes of cereal and 800 million liters of milk. FAO says they protected 36.6 million people's food security. The Times quotes FAO's USD 1.5 billion averted since February 2020. These are estimates for the whole operation; AI data handling was one part.

FAO received up to 2,500 records a day with nearly 25 percent unusable. PlantVillage's AI removed the unwanted data. Over 240,000 records were collected in a year from scouts and citizens who could not have used the discontinued eLocust3 tablets.
No individually documented farmer outcome in the sources.

ai_role.statement: Two AI uses are documented: algorithms that double-check submitted photos (Times) and AI that filters unusable records out of FAO's daily intake (FAO). A Penn State deep-learning soil-moisture model is mentioned by the maker's university. The outcome figures belong to the entire control operation and no source isolates the AI's contribution. FAO is both co-developer and deployer, so its feature is maker-authored. The Times report is independent with named sources (Cressman, Ferrand, Hughes, Jeptoo, Owuor, Craig).

fields.account: In early 2020 desert locust swarms swept the Horn of Africa. FAO's senior locust forecaster Keith Cressman asked Penn State's PlantVillage to adapt its app. PlantVillage had built FAO's fall armyworm app. eLocust3M was released on Google Play on 20 February 2020. Anyone with a smartphone could record georeferenced locust sightings; algorithms checked photos. Penn State also extended a deep-learning soil-moisture model to the affected region. FAO reported receiving up to 2,500 records a day, nearly 25 percent unusable or incorrect. It asked PlantVillage to use artificial intelligence to identify and remove the unwanted data before sharing locations with ground and air control teams. The New York Times reported over 240,000 records collected in a year by PlantVillage scouts, government personnel and citizens. The wider operation also used Garmin satellite devices, EarthRanger (Vulcan) and 28 aircraft coordinated with 51 Degrees. FAO's 6 May 2021 feature says East African control operations prevented the loss of 4 million tonnes of cereal and 800 million liters of milk. They protected 36.6 million people's food security and avoided USD 1.56 billion in losses, it says. The Times quoted FAO's estimate of USD 1.5 billion averted since February 2020. It quoted FAO's Cyril Ferrand saying swarms were prevented from spilling into the Sahel.

fields.summary: PlantVillage's app, built with FAO in under a month in 2020, gathered 240,000+ records; AI removed unusable data; FAO credits the tech-enabled operation with averting USD 1.56 billion in losses.
fields.account: In early 2020 desert locust swarms swept the Horn of Africa. FAO's senior locust forecaster Keith Cressman asked Penn State's PlantVillage to adapt its app. PlantVillage had built FAO's fall armyworm app. eLocust3M was released on Google Play on 20 February 2020. Anyone with a smartphone could record georeferenced locust sightings; algorithms checked photos. Penn State also extended a deep-learning soil-moisture model to the affected region. FAO reported receiving up to 2,500 records a day, nearly 25 percent unusable or incorrect. It asked PlantVillage to use artificial intelligence to identify and remove the unwanted data before sharing locations with ground and air control teams. The New York Times reported over 240,000 records collected in a year by PlantVillage scouts, government personnel and citizens. The wider operation also used Garmin satellite devices, EarthRanger (Vulcan) and 28 aircraft coordinated with 51 Degrees. FAO's 6 May 2021 feature says East African control operations prevented the loss of 4 million tonnes of cereal and 800 million liters of milk. They protected 36.6 million people's food security and avoided USD 1.56 billion in losses, it says. The Times quoted FAO's estimate of USD 1.5 billion averted since February 2020. It quoted FAO's Cyril Ferrand saying swarms were prevented from spilling into the Sahel.
